transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Yeah, hi. Thanks for fitting me in. So, um, I guess the main reason I'm here is... well, it's kind of a long story, but it has to do with my eating habits lately. 

See, I'm a firefighter, and I've been really busting my ass trying to get on the lieutenant track. It's incredibly competitive at my firehouse, and you really have to prove you're at peak performance, you know? Not just knowing all the protocols and leadership stuff, but physically, too. You have to be in absolute top shape. So, a while back, I decided I was going to start eating cleaner. Just, you know, cutting out the garbage the guys usually cook at the station, trying to optimize everything so I'd be lighter on my feet and have better endurance for the drills and the physical exams. 

But the thing is, what started as just eating cleaner has somehow turned into me constantly cutting my meals down. Like, it's gotten to the point where my whole day is just black coffee in the morning, maybe a protein shake in the afternoon, and then a really small dinner. And the part that's actually starting to mess with my head a little—and why I finally decided to make an appointment—is that I'm doing this even on my shift days. I mean, when you're on shift, you're hauling heavy hoses, wearing 70 pounds of turnout gear, going on back-to-back calls... I know for an absolute fact that I've burned way, way more than what I'm taking in with just some coffee and a shake. But I still just keep shrinking my meals down, and I just can't seem to stop doing it.
Are you afraid of gaining weight?

Yeah, I mean... it's not like I'm sitting around all day terrified of the number itself, but... well, actually, maybe I am. It's more about what the weight represents, you know? Like, at the station, everyone is always watching everyone else. It's a brotherhood, sure, but it's also a constant competition. We bust each other's chops about everything. And if I step on the scale in the locker room—which I do, probably more than I should, honestly, sometimes before and after shift, sometimes even in the middle if things are slow—and if that number is up even a pound... man, it just messes with my head. 

Like, maybe we had a big station meal the night before, because somebody made chili or whatever, or maybe I just drank a ton of water because we were out on a hot call. Rationally, I know that's just water weight or food in my stomach. I took anatomy and physiology for my EMT cert, I know how the body works. But in that moment, when I see that number tick up, I get this... this really tight, almost suffocating feeling in my chest. It's like this flash of panic. I immediately start thinking that I've completely blown it, that all my hard work is down the drain, and that the other guys are going to look at me and think I'm getting soft. Or worse, that the captain is going to think I'm losing my edge and lacking discipline, which is a death sentence if you're trying to make lieutenant. I just get so fixated on the idea that if I'm heavier, I'm slower, I'm weaker, I'm out of control. And I can't let them see me as out of control. I have to be the guy who has it all together, the guy who's dialed in. So yeah, I guess I am afraid of it. Really afraid of it. It just feels like if I gain weight, I'm failing at my job and failing myself.
Do you think your body would look unappealing if you gained weight?

Well, unappealing... I don't know if that's the exact word I'd use, but it's definitely tied up in how I see myself, especially in uniform. Like, every single morning before I head out to the station, I have this routine. I stand in front of the mirror in my bathroom—the lighting there is pretty harsh, actually, it really highlights everything—and I just stare at myself. I'm looking specifically at my waist and my face. I need to see that my jawline is sharp, that there's no puffiness, and that my waist is completely trim. Because if I look in that mirror and I feel like I look even a little bit soft, or if my face looks rounder than it did the day before, it completely ruins my headspace for the entire shift. 

It's like, if I don't look sharp and leaned out, I don't feel sharp. And in my line of work, especially going for lieutenant, you have to project this image of total authority and readiness. You have to look like the guy who can kick down a door and carry someone out of a burning building without breaking a sweat. So if I feel like my body doesn't reflect that—if I feel like I look heavier or softer—it completely messes with my confidence. I start second-guessing myself, wondering if the guys are looking at me thinking I don't have what it takes to lead them. I just don't feel command-ready, you know? It's like my physical appearance dictates my entire ability to do my job and be respected. So yeah, the idea of gaining weight and losing that edge, that sharpness... it really bothers me. It makes me feel like I'm not the firefighter I'm supposed to be.
Do you feel like you're in control when you're eating less and losing weight?

Yeah, I mean... I guess that's a big part of it, right? Control. Because honestly, the job is chaos. You never know what the next call is going to be. Could be a cat stuck in a tree, could be a five-alarm fire with people trapped inside. You just don't know. And even when you're not on a call, you're constantly at the mercy of the schedule, the alarm, the captain's moods... everything is so unpredictable. But this? This is something I can control. 

When I look at my plate and decide, "No, I'm not eating that," or when I push through a grueling shift on just a protein shake and some coffee, I feel... I don't know, powerful? Like I'm mastering my own body. It's like my body is this machine, and I'm the one programming it to run on absolute minimum fuel while still putting out maximum effort. And when I step on that scale and see the number go down, it's tangible proof. It's like a little victory in a day where I might not have control over anything else. 

I remember this one shift a few weeks ago, it was brutal. We had three back-to-back structure fires. I was exhausted, covered in soot, every muscle in my body was screaming. The guys ordered a bunch of pizzas when we finally got back to the station around 3 AM. The smell was incredible, and I was starving. I mean, my stomach was practically eating itself. But I sat there, drank a glass of water, and didn't touch a single slice. And as crazy as it sounds, sitting there, feeling that hunger but not giving into it... it felt better than eating the pizza would have. It felt like I was stronger than everyone else in that room who was stuffing their faces. It felt like discipline. 

So yeah, when I'm restricting what I eat and I see the weight dropping, it definitely gives me this huge sense of control. It's almost like a high, you know? Like I'm proving to myself that I have this ironclad willpower that nobody else has. And when you're trying to prove you have what it takes to be a lieutenant, to be a leader... having that kind of control over yourself feels like the most important thing in the world. It's just... lately, I'm starting to wonder if I'm the one in control, or if this whole thing is starting to control me. But in the moment? Yeah. It feels like pure control.
Do you think you would be able to stop restricting your food intake if you didn't care about your weight or body shape?

Man, that's... that's a really tough question. If I didn't care about my weight or how I looked in the uniform? I mean, it's so hard to even separate the two things in my head at this point. Because caring about the weight is just... it's the baseline, you know? It's like asking if I'd still check my turnout gear if I wasn't worried about getting burned in a fire. It's just what you do. 

But... if I somehow just magically stopped caring about my shape today? I honestly don't know if I could just flip a switch and start eating normally again. I really don't. Because it's become this whole ingrained routine now. Like, I have my exact schedule, and my brain is just wired for it. Wake up, black coffee, maybe a handful of almonds if I'm feeling shaky, then the shift, then a protein shake... it's so dialed in. It's literally muscle memory at this point. 

Just last Sunday, for example, my mom had my sister and me over for dinner. She does this once a month, and she made this huge pot roast, roasted potatoes, carrots, the works. And even though I was just sitting in her dining room, wearing a baggy sweater, not actively staring at a mirror or thinking about the captain or the guys at the station in that exact second... I still just couldn't bring myself to put the potatoes on my plate. My hand just wouldn't do it. My mom was giving me this look, you know the one, that worried mom look, and she kept trying to push the serving bowl toward me, saying I looked tired. And I just made up some excuse about having a late lunch with the guys. But really, it's just that the idea of eating it felt... wrong. Like I was breaking a fundamental rule of how I operate. 

So, if the weight thing wasn't a factor? I'm not sure. I'd like to think I could just sit down and eat a plate of food like a normal guy, but... the restricting, it's almost like it has a life of its own now. It's just how my day is structured. I don't even know if I'd know how to stop doing it, to be honest with you.
Do you think you would still want to restrict your food intake if you could maintain your current weight without doing so?

If I could just... magically maintain it? Like, if you could guarantee me that the number on the scale wouldn't budge no matter what I actually ate? Man, that... that sounds like a totally different world. Because right now, the fear of that number going up is just constantly hanging over me. It's like this shadow I can't ever really shake, no matter how much I try to rationalize it. 

I mean, the way things are now, if the scale is up even a pound—just one single pound—after a big station meal where I maybe couldn't get out of eating a few bites of whatever the guys cooked, or even just from drinking extra water... like, say we were running hose drills out in the July heat in full turnout gear and I'm just chugging water to stay upright... if I step on the scale later and see it's up even a fraction, I get this immediate, tight panic in my chest. It's a real physical reaction, like my throat closes up. I just feel like I’ve completely blown it. Like all my hard work and all that discipline I was talking about earlier is just ruined over a glass of water or a piece of chicken. 

And my brain just spirals from there. I immediately start thinking that people are going to notice, that they're going to see me as soft, or like I'm completely out of control of my own body. And in a firehouse, being seen as out of control or soft is basically a death sentence for your reputation, especially if you're aiming for lieutenant. You have to be the guy everyone can rely on, the one who has his act together one hundred percent of the time. You can't be the guy who's slipping. 

So I just obsess over that number to make sure I don't slip. If I didn't have that fear of gaining, if I knew for an absolute fact I'd just stay exactly as I am right now without having to skip meals or run on fumes... I'd like to think I wouldn't need to restrict like this. Because it's really that terror of gaining the weight, of putting on even an ounce and losing that edge and looking weak to the guys, that makes me keep such a tight grip on everything. It just consumes so much of my mental energy, constantly doing the math, constantly worrying if I'm going to look heavier tomorrow. It's exhausting, to be honest.
Is your desire to restrict food intake more about avoiding weight gain or about feeling in control of your body?

I mean, it's kind of what I was just getting at, you know? They’re so tangled up together in my head. But if I really have to sit here and pick which one is driving the bus... I think it’s the weight gain. It really is. 

Because the control feels good, sure, like I said before with the pizza and feeling disciplined. But the fear... that fear of the weight actually coming back on is what dictates my entire life right now. Like I was just saying about the scale—if I step on it in the locker room and it’s up even a single pound, even if I know logically it’s just from extra water after a heavy drill, I get that awful, tight panic in my chest. It’s not just 'oh, I lost control for a second.' It’s this overwhelming feeling of, 'I have completely blown it.' 

And my mind instantly jumps to how everyone at the station is going to see me. I just picture them looking at me, maybe noticing my jawline isn't as sharp or my uniform fits a little different, and thinking I'm getting soft, or that I can't hack it anymore. In our line of work, if you look like you're out of shape or letting yourself go, people lose respect for you fast. They think you're a liability. You're the guy who is going to run out of air first in a fire, or the guy who can't pull his own weight during an overhaul. 

So I guess... the control is really just my weapon against the weight gain, if that makes sense? The weight gain is the actual enemy. I use the control to make sure the weight doesn't happen. If I didn't have that deep-down terror about putting on pounds and looking weak or out of control to the rest of the crew, I don't think I'd need to grip the steering wheel so tight with every single thing I put in my mouth. It all just circles back to that panic of seeing the number go up.
Is there ever a time when you feel like you can relax and not worry about what you're eating?

Relax? Man, I... I really wish I could say yes, but no. Not really. Never, honestly. And I think... well, that's actually the whole reason I came in to see you in the first place. Because what started out as just me trying to eat cleaner, you know, to get in top shape for the lieutenant track—because they really look at your overall fitness and discipline when you're up for promotion—it's just completely snowballed. 

It started off fine, just cutting out the junk, but it's turned into me cutting my meals down to basically nothing. Like, my entire day is just black coffee in the morning, maybe a protein shake in the afternoon, and then a really small dinner. And the thing that really gets me, the part that makes me realize I can't ever just relax about it, is that I do this even on shift days. I mean, we'll be running calls back-to-back, hauling 70 pounds of gear up three flights of stairs in the dead of summer, swinging axes, and I know—I know for an absolute fact—that I burned way, way more energy than what I'm taking in. My body will be absolutely screaming for fuel. 

But even then, I still can't just sit down at the station table and eat a normal, relaxed meal with the guys. I'll be sitting there with my tiny, measured-out portion while they're housing a giant pasta bake or a bunch of burgers, and my brain is just buzzing, stressing over every single bite. Even when I'm totally exhausted and literally running on fumes, I can't turn that worry off and just eat. The anxiety about it is just always there, humming in the background, making sure I stick to the coffee and the shake. So, yeah, relaxing around food just isn't something that happens for me anymore.
Is your restrictive eating more about avoiding weight gain or feeling in control of your body when you're not thinking about your firefighter career?

Even if you take the job completely out of the picture... man, it's still the weight. I know I keep bringing it back to the firehouse, and I've probably talked your ear off about the guys and the station meals and all that, but... if I'm just at home, on my own time, completely away from the job? It's the exact same thing. It really is. 

Like I was saying before about the scale going up just a single pound and getting that tight, awful panic in my chest? That doesn't just happen in the locker room. If I'm standing in my own bathroom on a Sunday morning, and I haven't even thought about a fire truck in two days, and I step on that scale and see it tick up even a fraction... I still get that exact same feeling of just completely blowing it. My throat still gets tight. My heart still starts racing. 

And I still immediately start worrying that people—just people in general, not even my crew, but my friends, my family, girls I might date, whoever—are going to see me as soft or completely out of control of myself. I'll sit there on the edge of my bathtub and just absolutely spiral. I'll start running through everything I consumed the day before, trying to calculate where I messed up, even if it was literally just having an extra glass of water before bed or, I don't know, eating a few too many almonds while watching TV. 

So the control... I mean, feeling in control of my body is a nice byproduct, I guess. It makes me feel like I have my life together when other things are stressful. But the real monster in the closet, the thing that actually keeps me up at night and dictates every single choice I make, whether I'm in uniform or just in jeans and a t-shirt, is that number going up. It’s the sheer terror of being heavier, of looking softer, of being seen as someone who just let themselves go. The career just amplifies it, but that fear of gaining weight is always the one driving the car.
Do you think you would still want to restrict your food intake if you weren't a firefighter?

Honestly, doc, that's... it's hard to even separate the two in my head at this point. Because, like I was telling you a little bit ago, the whole reason I even made this appointment in the first place—the whole catalyst for this entire situation—was the job. It started with that lieutenant track. I really just wanted to eat cleaner, you know? Just optimize my performance, drop a little body fat, look the part so the brass would take me seriously when promotion time rolled around. 

But if you took the job away tomorrow? If I just handed in my turnout gear and, I don't know, went to work in an office or got a desk job somewhere? Yeah. Yeah, I really think I'd still be doing this. Because it's gone so far past just trying to look fit for a promotion. Like I said before, it’s turned into me cutting my meals down to basically nothing. I wake up, I have my black coffee, I might have a protein shake in the afternoon if I'm feeling really shaky, and then a really small dinner. That's my whole day. 

And the part that really proves to me that this is bigger than just being a firefighter is that I do this exact same routine even on my heavy shift days. Days where I am sweating through my gear, hauling hoses, doing overhaul for hours... I know for an absolute fact that I burned way, way more energy than what I'm taking in. I know my body is in a massive deficit. But I still can't bring myself to eat more. The fear of that scale moving up just completely overrides any logic or physical hunger. 

So if I'm doing that—if I'm strictly limiting myself to coffee and a shake on days when my body is physically screaming for fuel after fighting a fire—I can't imagine I'd magically start eating normal meals just because I changed careers. The restriction... it's like it has a life of its own now. It started with the firehouse, sure, but now it's just how my brain works, no matter what I'm doing.

I know I kind of just touched on this a minute ago, but... yeah, it’s really, definitely the weight. I mean, the control is nice, but it all comes back to avoiding the weight gain. Like I was saying about that feeling when the scale moves? It's... it's hard to even describe how intense it is. 

Let's say, just as an example, there’s a big station meal and I actually gave in and ate a little bit more than my usual tiny portion because the guys wouldn't let up, or... or honestly, even if I just drank some extra water because I was severely dehydrated from a fire the night before. If I wake up and step on that scale and it’s up even a single pound from that water or whatever, I get this... this incredibly tight panic right in my chest. It’s like all the air gets sucked out of the room. I instantly feel like I’ve completely blown it, like all my hard work is just ruined in one morning. 

And then my brain just starts spinning out of control, worrying that people are going to look at me and see me as soft. I get so paranoid that they'll think I'm just totally out of control of myself, you know? Like I'm just some guy who can't even maintain his own body. So... yeah, even when I'm not thinking about the job at all, that fear of gaining weight and looking soft is what's really driving all of this. It's just this constant, exhausting dread that never really shuts off, no matter where I am or what I'm doing.

I know we just went over this, and I feel like I'm repeating myself, but it really is the weight. I mean, I know I just said this, but it's hard to overstate how much it consumes my thoughts. Even if I'm nowhere near the firehouse, even if I'm just sitting on my couch on a Tuesday afternoon watching TV and not thinking about work at all... it's the weight. The control is a nice feeling, sure, but it's just a side effect of trying to keep the weight off. 

Like I was trying to explain before about the scale... it's just this overwhelming thing. Let's say I'm at the station, right? And it's someone's birthday or whatever, and they made this huge spread, and the guys are just relentless. "Come on, eat something, you're making us look bad," all that typical firehouse banter. And maybe I finally just cave and have a little bit more than my usual, tiny amount. Or, honestly, even if I just drink a ton of water because we had a bad run the night before and I was sweating through my gear for three hours straight and I'm just incredibly dehydrated. 

If I wake up the next morning, step on that scale in my bathroom, and it's up even a single pound—just one pound from water weight or whatever—I get this immediate, physical reaction. It's this tight, awful panic right in the center of my chest. It feels like I can't catch my breath. I just instantly feel like I have completely and utterly blown it. Like every single day of discipline and skipping meals and being hungry was just thrown out the window because of one stupid decision. 

And then the thoughts start spiraling. I start thinking about how people are going to look at me. I worry that they're going to see me and think I look soft, or that I've just let myself go. I get so paranoid that they'll think I'm totally out of control of my own body, you know? Like I'm weak. So, yeah, it's not about feeling in control of my life, it's about not being seen as someone who is out of control of their body, if that makes sense. It's the fear of gaining weight, 100 percent. It just never stops.

Doc, I... I feel like I'm a broken record here, man. I really don't know how else to phrase this because I feel like we're just going in circles on this exact same question. But I'll try to break it down again. 

It is absolutely, fundamentally about the weight. It's not about feeling in control of my life or my emotions or whatever else when I'm off the clock. In fact, I don't feel in control at all when I step on that scale. It's the exact opposite. 

Like I’ve been trying to tell you, if I'm at the firehouse and I end up having a bigger portion at a station meal just to get the guys off my back, or—and this is the craziest part to me—even if I just chug a bunch of extra water because we had a brutal, hot run and I'm severely dehydrated... if I wake up the next morning and that digital scale ticks up even one single, solitary pound, I don't feel powerful. I get this immediate, suffocating, tight panic right in the middle of my chest. It's a very real, physical reaction. 

I just stand there staring at the number, and my brain just screams that I've completely blown it. Like every single day of discipline was just ruined by one glass of water or one extra bite of chicken. And it all stems from this absolute terror that if I start gaining weight, people are going to look at me and think, "Wow, he's getting soft." I just have this constant, gnawing anxiety that they'll look at me and think I lack discipline, like I'm totally out of control of my own physical body and I'm letting myself go. 

So, no, it's not about controlling my life outside of work. It’s entirely, 100 percent about avoiding the weight gain so I don't look soft. That's the fear. The weight is the whole thing. Does that... does that make more sense now? Because I really don't know how else to explain it to you.
Is your restrictive eating habit something you think you would still have if you weren't worried about how you look to others?

That's... well, I guess that's a slightly different angle than what we were just talking about. Because as much as I talk about the guys at the station and not wanting to look soft to them, honestly? If I were totally alone, if no one else was ever going to look at me again... I really think I'd still be doing exactly what I'm doing. Because at the end of the day, it's not just their eyes on me, it's my own eyes. 

Let me just give you a rundown of how my mornings go, every single day, without fail. Before I even put my uniform on, before I even go into the kitchen to make a black coffee, I have this whole routine in the bathroom. I stand there in front of the mirror, and I just scrutinize myself. I'm looking at very specific things. I turn to the side, I pull my shirt tight or take it off, and I focus entirely on my waist. I need to see if it looks tight, if it's sharp. And then I lean in close to the glass and I check my face, right around the jawline and cheeks, just looking for any puffiness or softness from the day before. 

I'll stand there for, I don't know, ten, sometimes twenty minutes just checking the angles. And if I look in that mirror before work and I feel like my waist and my face don't look sharp enough... man, it just completely derails me. It totally messes with how confident I feel for the rest of the shift. As a firefighter, you have to be ready to step up, take charge of a scene, and project authority. You have to be decisive. But if I don't pass that mirror test in the morning, I just don't feel command-ready at all. I feel sluggish, I feel insecure, like I'm faking it. I'll spend the whole shift second-guessing myself on calls just because I felt like my jawline looked a little soft at 5:00 AM. 

So, yeah, it's definitely about other people to an extent, but the restriction... it's mostly so I can actually face myself in the mirror and feel like I'm sharp enough to do my job. If I didn't restrict, I wouldn't ever feel ready to walk out my front door.
Would you still feel the need to restrict your food intake if you were alone on a deserted island with no possibility of being seen by others?

Doc, seriously, are you even listening to me? I feel like I'm talking to a brick wall here, man. A deserted island is exactly what I just meant when I said if I were totally alone and no one was ever going to look at me again. But... fine, okay, let's play out the deserted island scenario. 

Yes. A hundred percent yes, I would still restrict my food. Because it goes right back to what I literally just spent the last five minutes explaining to you about my morning routine. It is a deeply internal thing. Even if I was stranded in the middle of nowhere, I would probably be staring into a tide pool or finding a piece of reflective glass every single morning just to check myself. 

Because like I just said, when I look in the mirror before work—or before whatever I'd be doing on this island—I am zeroing in on whether my waist and my face look sharp enough. That is the baseline for my entire day. If I check my waist and it feels soft, or if my face looks even a tiny bit puffy, it completely destroys my confidence. I told you, it messes with how command-ready I feel. 

And you might be sitting there thinking, well, why do you need to feel command-ready on an island with no fires to put out and no crew to lead? Because it's a state of mind! It's how I exist in my own body. If I don't have that physical sharpness, I feel physically heavy, I feel sluggish, I feel completely incapable of making a single basic decision. My brain just turns to mush. I have to see that tightness in my shape, I have to know that my jawline is sharp and my waist is completely flat, or I just can't function, period. It doesn't matter who is or isn't looking at me. I'm looking at me. Does that finally answer it?
Would your desire to restrict food intake change if you no longer felt the need to prove yourself to others?

Doc... I honestly... is this a test? Is this one of those psychiatric techniques where you just keep rephrasing the exact same question to see if my story changes? Because I swear, I am trying so hard to be patient here, but we are literally just running in circles. 'Prove myself to others' is just the deserted island question dressed up in a different shirt. 

But fine. Fine, I will explain it again. No, my desire to restrict would not change one single bit if I didn't have to prove myself to anyone else. Because the only person I am desperately trying to prove anything to is the guy staring back at me in the bathroom glass. 

Like I literally just said two minutes ago, when I look in that mirror before work, my entire focus—my whole morning, really—is about whether my waist and my face look sharp enough. That's the test. If I pull my shirt tight and my waist isn't perfectly flat, or if I turn my head and my face doesn't look completely sharp and chiseled... it just completely ruins me. It entirely messes with how confident and command-ready I feel for that day. It’s not about proving to my captain or the other guys on the rig that I can do my job, it’s about proving to *myself* that I have the discipline to even exist in my own skin. 

If I don't have that physical sharpness, I feel like a total fraud. I feel heavy and useless. So no, taking other people's opinions or expectations out of the equation doesn't fix this. I'd still be restricting, I'd still be standing in front of that mirror for twenty minutes checking my waist, I'd still be obsessing over my jawline, because I have to prove to *me* that I'm sharp enough to face the day. I really, really need you to hear what I'm saying this time, Doc, because I don't think I can explain this to you a fifth time. Can we please move on to something else?
Would you still feel the need to restrict your food intake if you were in a situation where you had complete privacy and there was no possibility of anyone judging your appearance?

Doc... are you kidding me right now? Complete privacy? No possibility of anyone judging me? I feel like I'm losing my mind here, man. That is literally—and I mean *literally*—the exact same question you just asked me three different ways. I don't know if you're writing this down, or if you're just waiting for your turn to speak, or if this is some kind of psychological endurance test, but I'm going to say this one more time. And I'll use as many words as it takes until it actually sinks in. 

It does not matter if I am in a crowded firehouse, a deserted island, or a completely private, locked, windowless bunker where no human being will ever lay eyes on me again. Because even in that bunker, I'm going to find a mirror, or a piece of glass, or a puddle of water. 

I know I keep bringing up the mirror routine, but I need you to understand that it is the absolute center of my entire day. When I look in the mirror before work, even if I'm the only person on earth, my entire existence in that moment boils down to whether my waist and my face look sharp enough. That is the whole ballgame. I am standing there, in complete privacy, pulling my shirt tight, pinching the skin, turning my head to check the angles of my jaw, looking for any softness. And if they don't look sharp, if there is even a millimeter of puffiness, it completely messes with how confident and command-ready I feel for that day. 

You keep talking about other people judging me. I don't care about other people judging me! I am the harshest judge! No one else is inspecting my face at 5:00 AM. But *I* know. If I don't see that sharpness, my brain just short-circuits. I can't lead a team, I can't make split-second decisions on a call, I can't even trust myself to hold a hose line properly because I feel so sluggish and out of control in my own body. Privacy changes absolutely nothing.
